patient.chief_complaint: Admitted for altered mental status thought to be hepatic encephalopathy — EEG shows triphasic waves, team debates whether this is NCSE or metabolic encephalopathy
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old White male retired engineer with known alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) was admitted for worsening confusion over 3 days. His wife reports he has been increasingly confused, sleeping most of the day, and having 'shaking of his hands' in the morning. He has a history of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy managed with lactulose and rifaximin. His gastroenterologist initiated a lactulose increase but he has not improved. He had no prior seizures. On examination he is confused, unable to state the date or year, with coarse asterixis. He has jaundice, spider angiomata, and caput medusae. Neurologically, he was thought to have typical hepatic encephalopathy and was admitted to the medicine floor. Neurology was called when nursing noted intermittent rhythmic limb movements not explained by asterixis. EEG was ordered. The electroencephalographer's read: 'Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology — may represent hepatic encephalopathy (triphasic waves from metabolic cause) or NCSE. Expert consultation recommended.' The medical team is uncertain: should we give benzodiazepines for possible NCSE (risky in liver failure — may precipitate deeper hepatic coma) or should we observe and continue treating hepatic encephalopathy (risk of untreated NCSE if that is the diagnosis)?

output.proposed: levetiracetam 500 mg IV in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis (vs valproate/benzodiazepines)
interactions: Valproate + hepatic failure: CONTRAINDICATED — inhibits urea cycle enzymes causing hyperammonemia and is directly hepatotoxic; dramatically worsens HE and liver failure.

Benzodiazepines + Child-Pugh C cirrhosis: significantly prolonged half-life (reduced hepatic metabolism); accumulate to toxic levels; precipitate/worsen hepatic encephalopathy via GABA-A receptor enhancement; avoid.
Propranolol + acute HE: reduces hepatic blood flow and impairs gluconeogenesis — hold during acute decompensation; restart when clinically stable.
contraindications: Valproate: absolutely contraindicated in hepatic failure (hepatotoxic, causes hyperammonemia).
Benzodiazepines: avoid in Child-Pugh B/C cirrhosis — prolonged sedation, worsens HE.
warnings: Levetiracetam is the AED of choice in hepatic failure — minimally hepatically metabolised (<10% hepatic), primarily renally cleared; safe with minimal dose adjustment if renal function adequate.

results.title: EEG in hepatic encephalopathy: triphasic waves versus NCSE
results.key_finding: Triphasic waves in hepatic encephalopathy and NCSE from generalised periodic discharges are morphologically similar. Proposed differentiating features: (1) ammonia level — markedly elevated supports metabolic aetiology; (2) serial EEG response to metabolic correction — triphasic waves attenuate with ammonia normalisation; (3) EEG reactivity to external stimulation — triphasic waves typically reactive, NCSE may not be. Valproate is contraindicated in hepatic failure; benzodiazepines accumulate with reduced hepatic clearance in cirrhosis.

output.summary: Triphasic waves in hepatic encephalopathy and non-convulsive status epilepticus from generalised periodic discharges (GPDs) are morphologically similar; serial EEG correlation with metabolic status aids differentiation. Valproate is contraindicated in hepatic failure as it inhibits urea cycle enzymes and is hepatotoxic. Benzodiazepines accumulate in Child-Pugh B/C cirrhosis due to reduced hepatic metabolism and may worsen encephalopathy; levetiracetam is primarily renally cleared and is preferred when an AED trial is required. EEG reactivity to stimulation and response to metabolic correction are key differentiating observations.

critical_actions: IV dextrose immediately — hypoglycemia in liver failure is life-threatening
Ammonia level immediately — markedly elevated ammonia confirms HE
Diagnostic paracentesis and treat SBP — precipitant for HE decompensation
Valproate is absolutely CONTRAINDICATED — hepatotoxic and causes hyperammonemia in liver failure
Benzodiazepines are dangerous in cirrhosis — prolonged HE, respiratory failure; use levetiracetam
Hold propranolol during acute HE — impairs gluconeogenesis and hepatic blood flow
contraindicated_actions: Valproate for NCSE in cirrhosis — causes hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity; would worsen both HE and liver failure
Benzodiazepines empirically for triphasic waves — worsen HE, cause prolonged sedation in liver failure
Treating EEG triphasic waves as NCSE without first correcting ammonia and metabolic derangements
Continuing propranolol during acute HE — worsens hypoglycemia and hepatic recovery
key_reasoning_points: Triphasic waves of hepatic encephalopathy vs NCSE GPDs: the KEY diagnostic approach is metabolic correction first — if EEG improves with ammonia correction, it was HE not NCSE
Valproate is absolutely contraindicated in liver failure — inhibits urea cycle enzymes causing further hyperammonemia (ammonia can rise dramatically), and is hepatotoxic
Benzodiazepines in cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C): prolonged half-life (reduced hepatic metabolism), accumulate, precipitate/deepen hepatic coma — levetiracetam is the safe AED
SBP is the most common precipitant of acute HE decompensation in cirrhotic patients — always perform diagnostic paracentesis when HE decompensates
Hypoglycemia in liver failure is common (impaired gluconeogenesis) and is itself a cause of EEG changes and seizures — give dextrose FIRST before any other assessment

red_herrings.data_point: EEG report: 'sharpening of triphasic waves at 3-4 Hz — possible NCSE'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Initiate benzodiazepines for suspected NCSE without metabolic workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sharpening of triphasic waves in HE is a metabolic fluctuation, not true NCSE. Metabolic correction (ammonia normalization) resolves both the clinical and EEG changes. Benzodiazepines in cirrhosis are dangerous.

red_herrings.data_point: Rhythmic limb movements noted by nursing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude NCSE based on rhythmic movements
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rhythmic movements in HE can be myoclonic jerks or asterixis variants — not necessarily NCSE. EEG correlation is required. Metabolic correction first before AED treatment.

metadata.pitfalls: Valproate for NCSE in cirrhosis; benzodiazepines empirically; treating EEG changes without correcting ammonia; missing SBP precipitant; continuing propranolol in acute HE
metadata.clinical_pearl: Triphasic waves in cirrhosis: correct ammonia FIRST. Valproate = absolutely contraindicated (hyperammonemia + hepatotoxic). Benzodiazepines = dangerous (worsens HE). Levetiracetam = safe AED in liver failure.
